turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Right, I've popped the cuff on. Blood pressure is 138 over 84, pulse 72, oxygen 98. Doctor Okonkwo's just washing her hands.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ta love. Um, is 138 decent? Factory medical had me at one fifty over ninety odd, that's why they stuck me on the water tablet.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Today's one is fine. My sister's blood pressure went daft after her third, she's on three different tablets, but that's her not you.
[SEG0004] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hello, I'm Dr Okonkwo. Come and sit. What's been the trouble?

[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): It's me hands. At night the thumb, the index and the middle finger go numb, both sides but the right is miles worse, and I have to shake them to wake them up. Feels like I've overdone it on the packing line.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long has that been going on, and does it actually wake you?

[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, maybe six weeks, could be longer, I can't pin it. Wakes me two or three times a night. I flap the hand and it eases off after a minute or so. Daytime I'm mostly alright unless I'm gripping boxes.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): Have you been dropping things?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah I've started dropping cups. Smashed my Blackpool mug last Tuesday, wife was furious. Nearly lost the kettle as well. Sorry, I'm rambling.

[SEG0010] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I've clocked it too. I come three mornings a week for his dad, I'm his dad's carer not his, and twice this month a cup's just gone out of his hand. My own wrists are fine, my daughter's a hairdresser and she's the one always on about her hands.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Does the numbness travel up the arm at all, or is there neck pain?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No, it stays in those three fingers. Neck's fine. Honestly I can't hear myself think on that line, the machines are brutal, but that's just noise, my hearing's alright.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any numbness or tingling in the feet?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No, feet are fine. Mornings though I feel like a wet rag, from the broken sleep I reckon. Once I've had a brew I'm alright.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any aching in the hand itself?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): A bit, yeah, more of an ache in the right wrist and palm at the end of a shift. I take a couple of Nurofen for it, the 200 milligram ones, not every day.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the water tablet, do you know the proper name and the dose?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Err, bendroflumethazide, the water tablet. 2.5 milligrams, one in the morning. Little white tablet. Been on it a couple of years for the blood pressure.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Bendroflumethiazide 2.5 milligrams, yes. Any other regular medicines?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No, just that and the odd Nurofen. I pack biscuits, been on that line fifteen years. Oh I used to smoke, packed it in when the factory went smoke free, years back now.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines, plasters, anything?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing I know of.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any operations on the hands or wrists before?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. Closest I've come is a splinter off a pallet. Daft, really.
[SEG0025] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I only catch the mornings. My sister had wrist trouble years ago and she still goes on about it, but that's her, nothing to do with him.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me have a look at the hands. No wasting in the palm muscles. I'm going to tap over the wrist.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mm. That tap on the right sends a tingle into the thumb and middle finger. Left side doesn't. Grip on the right is a little weaker than the left.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah that tap was weird, like a little shock. Reminds me of the static off the shrink wrap, we have a laugh about it on shift.

[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): What I think is going on is carpal tunnel. The median nerve runs through a tight tunnel at the wrist, and at night when the wrist bends the pressure squashes the nerve, so those three fingers go numb. Shaking the hand eases it a bit. Working impression, not a definite label yet.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. So I'm not falling apart. The lads at work said it was arthritis and I nearly had a panic in the canteen.

[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): I wouldn't call it arthritis from what I can see. A neutral wrist splint at night, not a tight bandage, often settles this. Buy one at the chemist and wear it every night for the next few weeks.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Every night, even weekends? I sleep with my hands under the pillow. And the dog hogs the bed, useless animal.

[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes, especially then, it stops the wrist curling under the pillow. If the splint hasn't helped, we might send you for nerve conduction tests to check the nerve. Not booking that today.
[SEG0034] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'll nag him about the splint when I'm in with his dad. I forget my own tablets half the time, the blood pressure ones, so I'm a fine one to talk.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let's see you back in six weeks either way, and we'll check how the nights are.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks, yeah. Should I ease off the Nurofen? They help the ache but I don't want to mess my stomach. Canteen curry is already a gamble.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Short courses with food are fine if your stomach stays happy. Don't take them every day for weeks. If you get heartburn or black stools, stop and let us know.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Stomach's been fine, touch wood. I'll grab the splint on the way home. Cheers for not rushing me, I do go on.
[SEG0039] person_1 (NURSE): Chemist on the corner usually has them. My boy wears a wrist support for his boxing, completely different, ignore me.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Ha, boxing. Right, I'll leave you in peace.
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): Take care, and do wear it nightly. See you in six weeks.

spec.situation: Middle-aged office or factory worker with night-time numbness in thumb, index and middle fingers, shakes hands to wake them; dropping cups; splint advice, nerve test conditional.

traps.happens: The patient describes things in colourful or sentence-like speech ('I've overdone it', 'I can't hear myself think', 'a frog in my throat', 'my feet feel dead', 'I feel like a wet rag').
traps.label_rule: Every symptom name is a short clinical noun phrase of 1 to 5 words ('voice fatigue', 'numbness in both feet', 'tiredness'), never a full sentence, never starting with I/we/my. Pure idioms that are not symptoms ('I can't hear myself think' said about classroom noise) are NOT symptoms. The patient's own words stay in the cited turn, not in the name.

traps.happens: The doctor (or nurse) explains a mechanism or a diagnosis in the patient's body ('the voice box is irritated by reflux', 'diabetes dulls the nerves in the feet', 'the swelling is your body fighting infection'). A nurse or caregiver also mentions a fact about THEIR OWN life (their sister, their child, their own illness).
traps.label_rule: Explanations by the doctor are NEVER symptoms, history or social history of the patient; they may only appear as clinical_assessment or counselling if the doctor stated them as such. A nurse's or caregiver's own life facts are not recorded as the patient's. Each symptom's reported_by is the person who really described it.

features: colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.
hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.

omissions.text: Finger numbness wakes the patient from sleep two or three times a night.
No other regular medicines apart from bendroflumethiazide and occasional Nurofen.
Doctor advised the patient to let the practice know if Nurofen causes heartburn or black stools.
Follow-up was planned in six weeks either way specifically to check how the nights are.
